newsitem.title: USA: LG Semicon turns focus from 16-meg DRAM.
newsitem.headline: LG Semicon turns focus from 16-meg DRAM.

text.p: SAN FRANCISCO, Jan 29 (REUTER) - LG Semicon's America unit said Wednesday the company decided to shift some manufacturing resources out of 16-megabit memory chip production, which could result "over a period of time" in reducing its 16-meg output.

LG Semicon, a major worldwide producer of 16-meg dynamic random access memory chips most commonly installed in personal computers, said it was a business decision based on the current oversupply of 16-meg DRAMS in the market.
"The company has decided to reallocate its resources into other products besides the commodity 16-meg DRAM. We're going to accelerate 64-meg DRAMs," Arun Kamat, marketing director, said.
He said LG Semicon will use some of the chip fabrication plants used for 16-meg DRAM production for the 64-meg chips, particularly for asynchronous DRAM flash memory chips.
But LG Semicon will continue to produce 16-megabit DRAMS, Kamat said, both to support its customers and supply the market.
"The 16-meg is a mainstream commodity used in all mainstream PCs" he said "But the next generation DRAM is 64-meg and the 64 meg is gaining acceptance."
Kamat said the decision came out of LG Semicon's corporate headquarters in South Korea. The San Jose-based U.S. unit heard of the decision late last week, he said.
Kamat said the pace of LG Semicon's shift of resources to 64-meg DRAMS and its 16-meg output declines "depends on how quickly we can develop markets for these other products."
Rumors have circulated among stock market traders for days that several South Korean chip companies plan to cut back production of 16-meg DRAMS.

"There is clearly an oversupply of product," Kamat said "There's been some stability over the last month or so but demand has not kicked in to the degree that supply and demand will be in equilibrium. We believe that there is ...better market potential for these other products."
Hyundai Corp's U.S.-based Hyundai Electronics is also rumored to be cutting back production.
But officials in San Jose did not return phone calls seeking to confirm reports.

Earlier this week, the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association forecasted that Korea memory chip exports will fall 10.2 percent to $8.8 billion in 1997 from an estimated $9.8 billion in 1996 based on expectations of continued falling prices. The association expects the price of 16-meg DRAMS falling to $6 per unit. In 1996, prices plunged to $8 in the fourth quarter from around $34 in the first quarter, it said.
